purpose: Repeat optional automatic source-format adaptation with a one-second down-hold in direct and adaptive MediaMTX delivery
scope: One private profile changes only downHold from 3s to 1s relative to the recorded revision's formats/config.automatic.yaml. All six cases use identical media image digests.

Direct shapes producer-to-browser capacity; MediaMTX shapes only producer-to-adapter capacity. Both run on an isolated Docker bridge with real rstream signaling. This is not forced-TURN qualification.

The runner verifies actual decoded dimensions/cadence, source quality observations, single session, source bitrate recovery, bounded playback disruption and resource teardown. No playback gate is relaxed.
Total browser freeze counters include warmup. Phase and transition summaries keep their original measurements, including transition frame drops.

Resource CPU is measured as a fraction of one core from cgroups on this Docker Desktop host. Phase averages include transitions; they are not isolated steady-format benchmarks or embedded-target performance claims.
There is no pixel latency probe. The performance-environment gate checks socket-buffer warnings, not host scheduling. Historical failed runs retain their original verdicts.

findings: Five of six complete runs pass: all three direct cases and two of three MediaMTX cases. The final MediaMTX case fails only playback with a 0.208-second recovery freeze.

All six automatic ladders change 720p30 to 360p15 and return through 540p24 to 720p30. Their format, bitrate-response, source-target-recovery and resource-lifecycle gates pass. No steady constrained-network freeze is observed.

Initial transition disruption ranges from 1.220 to 1.868 seconds directly and 1.055691 to 1.469 seconds through MediaMTX. The second and third MediaMTX runs each drop two frames during that transition; these are included in disruption. The second also has 0.219 seconds of warmup freeze.

The last failure occurs after the large format is confirmed, with a stable 6000 kbit/s encoder target and no sampled downstream packet-loss/NACK increase. Its frame callback gap is 233.3 ms, receive-metadata gap 211.1 ms and JavaScript timer delay 167.1 ms. This coincides with the repeatedly observed UTC minute-ending-9, second-52.5 event; correlation does not identify its cause.

The whole series remains failed. The public three-second down-hold is unchanged. Inspect the periodic scheduling observation before changing media policy or starting another identical repetition series.
